analysis.one_liner: Requires colleges to provide confidential advisors, uniform sexual assault disciplinary procedures, and public safety data, with fines for noncompliance.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support from 10 senators, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every college that takes federal funds to designate trained, confidential sexual assault coordinators students can report to anonymously, run one uniform disciplinary process for all sexual misconduct cases regardless of who the accused is (for example, no separate track for athletes), and publish detailed data on how rape and fondling reports move through campus discipline. It also would have created a public, searchable Education Department website showing pending Title IX investigations and enforcement outcomes, given students amnesty from alcohol and drug violations when they report assault in good faith, and offered grants of up to $500,000 to help schools—especially those with small endowments—build prevention and victim services. Colleges that failed to comply could face civil penalties of up to 1% of their operating budget each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Students, especially survivors of campus sexual assault, dating violence, stalking, and harassment, gain a confidential person to report to, guaranteed accommodations (like changing housing or class schedules) without being forced to involve police, amnesty from alcohol or drug discipline when they report, and written notice of disciplinary proceedings within 24 hours for both sides. Prospective students and families gain a public website showing each school's Title IX coordinator, open federal investigations, and enforcement results, plus expanded campus crime statistics that track cases through the disciplinary process, including outcomes and sanctions. Colleges with small endowments or low tuition, tribal colleges, and historically Black colleges get grant preference for prevention and victim services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and campus sexual assault survivors

how_it_helps.text: Every college must appoint trained, confidential 'sexual and interpersonal violence coordinators' to whom students can report anonymously; these coordinators arrange accommodations like housing or schedule changes without requiring the student to involve police or triggering an investigation, and cannot be forced to report crimes in a way that identifies the student.

Colleges must use one uniform campus-wide disciplinary process for sexual misconduct cases and may not run a different process based on a student's status, such as membership on an athletic team, and must give both the accuser and the accused written notice of proceedings within 24 hours of a decision to proceed.

The Education Department must build a public, searchable campus safety website listing each school's Title IX coordinator, pending investigations, enforcement actions, and resolution agreements, and schools must report far more detail on rape and fondling cases through the Clery Act, including how many cases were disciplined, the findings, and the sanctions imposed.

Students who report sexual assault in good faith cannot be punished by the school for alcohol or drug violations revealed in the report, removing a common fear that keeps students from coming forward.

Colleges can win competitive grants of up to $500,000 for prevention research and victim services, with preference for schools with the smallest endowments or lowest tuition and for tribal colleges and historically Black colleges, and schools found in violation of Title IX or the Clery Act cannot receive the grants.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities pay. They would bear the cost of hiring and training coordinators, retraining everyone involved in disciplinary proceedings, building websites and reporting systems, and compiling expanded statistics—and face civil penalties of up to 1% of their operating budget per year of noncompliance. They also lose control over the reputational shield of keeping Title IX investigations and disciplinary outcomes out of public view.

drawbacks.text: Colleges face real compliance costs and potentially large fines: the bill lets the Education Department impose a civil penalty of up to 1% of a school's operating budget for each year it fails to meet the coordinator or other requirements, a burden that falls hardest on small schools even though those under 1,000 students may share a coordinator with neighboring institutions.

The grant program has no dedicated funding: grants are awarded only 'as funds become available through the payment of penalties' by violating colleges, so the money available for prevention depends on schools breaking the rules.

Protections arrive slowly: the coordinator requirement takes effect at the earliest 1 year after the Education Department settles staffing rules through negotiated rulemaking, and no later than 3 years after enactment, so students would wait years for the confidential advisor guarantee.

Anonymous reports carry no obligation to act: a college is only required to investigate a specific crime if the student formally reports it to a campus official or law enforcement, so the anonymous reporting system documents patterns but does not itself start a case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students, the benefits are concrete and the costs are borne almost entirely by institutions: confidential reporting, guaranteed accommodations, a single disciplinary process no athlete can bypass, and public data that lets applicants compare schools. The strongest honest objections are design flaws rather than the goals: penalty-funded grants are an unstable way to finance prevention, the phase-in is slow, and small colleges face compliance burdens, though the bill includes sharing arrangements for schools under 1,000 students. On balance, the costs fall on the institutions whose handling of these cases the bill is trying to fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced by Senator Gillibrand with nine cosponsors from both parties, but the Senate education committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Campus Accountability and Safety Act on September 29, 2022, with nine cosponsors including four Republicans—Grassley, Capito, Rubio, and Ernst—and five Democrats.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which is the last action ever taken on it.
The committee held no markup, reported no vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and universities came out ahead: they avoided new staffing mandates, public disclosure of Title IX investigations and disciplinary outcomes, and civil penalties of up to 1% of their operating budgets. Students gained nothing from the protections the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had genuinely bipartisan sponsorship—a Democratic lead sponsor joined by 5 of 48 Senate Democrats and 4 of 50 Senate Republicans—but no votes were ever taken, so no partisan divide was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill imposes staffing, training, reporting, and website requirements and allows civil penalties of up to 1% of an institution's operating budget per year of noncompliance. It also ends the ability of schools to keep Title IX investigations and campus disciplinary outcomes out of public view, and bars schools found in violation from receiving the bill's safety grants. Inaction on the bill spared institutions these costs.

industries.industry: Community-based victim services and rape crisis centers
industries.note: The bill encourages colleges to partner with rape crisis centers and other victim services organizations to serve as confidential coordinators, and grant funds may support partnerships with community-based victim services agencies.
